newsitem.title: UK: Man raises estimate for EU 1996/97 sugar output.
newsitem.headline: Man raises estimate for EU 1996/97 sugar output.

text.p: Trade house E D & F Man on Tuesday raised its estimate for European Union (EU) sugar production in 1996/97 by almost 300,000 tonnes to 15.63 million tonnes white value after a late boost from favourable weather. In September Man put EU 96/97 output at 15.34 million.
"The long mild autumn across much of western Europe has apparently given many of the beet crops a late boost," Man said.

"This year the period after the conclusion of the beet tests seems to have had a greater than usual significance for the final sugar contents," it said, adding that a number of campaigns started a few days late to benefit from the weather.
The EU produced 15.61 million tonnes in 1995/96, it said.
Man raised its forecasts for at least three key EU sugar producers, although said it had left most of its estimates unchanged. It has yet to release details of all the revisions.

In France, the EU's largest producer, production was still expected to be lower than last year's 4.2 million tonnes but higher than expected sugar contents prompted an upward revision of 100,000 tonnes to 4.05 million tonnes.
"The fall in beet area combined with a dry spring, that limited beet development, has meant that although sugar contents are good, average beet yields are lower," Man said.
The Belgian crop appeared to have benefited particularly well from the favourable autumn weather.
The latest estimates pegged the Belgian crop at 960,000 tonnes, 50,000 tonnes higher than Man's previous estimate and 73,000 higher than the outturn in 1995/96, it said.
Man raised its estimate for German sugar output by 100,000 tonnes to 4.05 million tonnes, the same as the French estimate.
Sugar contents in German beets were better than anticipated, averaging 18 percent, and beet deliveries were also well ahead of last season, it said.
In Britain, autumn weather was reported to have been particularly favourable for late beet development and sugar contents were very high.
Man increased its estimate of British sugar production by 50,000 tonnes to 1.3 million tonnes, an improvement on last year's result of almost 40,000 tonnes.
